title: Neighbors
hookLine: the people next door are the first neighbors
tomorrow: what if the stranger at your door is an angel?

cards: The delivery driver knows your front door better than the people on either side of it.
Hold that thought, because in Luke a lawyer asks Jesus a question that sounds like a legal search: in the Douay-Rheims Bible, "And who is my neighbour?" Who counts? Where's the line?
Jesus tells a story, and then does something odd. He never answers the question. He hands back a different one.
Why answer a question with a question?

teach.h: THE PRIEST, THE LEVITE, THE SAMARITAN.
teach.b: The story: a man going down from Jerusalem to Jericho is beaten, stripped and left half dead. A priest comes by and passes on the other side. So does a Levite.
Luke doesn't give their reasons, and they aren't cartoon villains. Then a Samaritan comes along, someone from a people the man's own people kept apart from, and he's moved with compassion.

He bandages the wounds, puts the man on his own animal, pays the innkeeper, and promises to come back. Now the twist. Jesus asks: which of these three was a neighbor to the man who fell among robbers?
The lawyer asked who counts as my neighbor, a boundary. Jesus asks who became one. Neighbor isn't a category you check people against.
It's something you do. And notice who does it. Jesus tells this to a man who knows the law by heart, and the one who lives it out on the road is the outsider, the one from across the line.
In Luke, mercy doesn't check where you're from.

teach.h: GO, AND DO THOU IN LIKE MANNER.
teach.b: The lawyer answers, the one who showed him mercy, and Jesus says, "Go, and do thou in like manner." So why start next door? Notice the Samaritan didn't go looking for a cause.
The man was lying on the road he was already traveling.
And the first road anyone travels runs past their own front door.
The people next door aren't more important than anyone else. They're simply first in line on your road.

how: Catholics hear the Good Samaritan read at Mass, and count care for the people around them among the works of mercy.

o: the people on your road, starting with those next door
only the people who share your street and town
people from your parish who you see on Sunday

games.q: on the road to Jericho — tap the pairs.

s: the Samaritan already knew the man on the road
he was a stranger from a people kept apart; he simply came along the road.
Jesus ends the story by asking which of the three was a neighbor
he turns who counts? into who became one?
Luke explains why the priest and the Levite passed by
Luke gives no reasons. they aren't cartoon villains; the story just shows who stopped.

games.q: a new family moves in across the hall. they speak a language you don't. going by Jesus's flipped question, what's the move?
o: wait until they reach out, so you don't intrude.
knock, smile, and bring something small to say hello.
find out first whether they share your faith.
games.why: Jesus doesn't ask who counts; he asks who became a neighbor. language and faith didn't stop the Samaritan.

practice: Listen for the sounds of the people around you: a door, footsteps upstairs, a car pulling in, a dog, a voice through the wall. Each sound is a person on your road.
As each one comes, let it be a quiet hello, and notice which ones you could put a name to.

wordCard.voice: Neighbors. Not a category to check people against, but something you become, starting with the people next door. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: neighbor, the Vulgate's word for the lawyer's question in Luke 10.

carryVoice: Your line: next door. The Samaritan's road was the one he was already on. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: Go, and do thou in like manner.
